kurals.tamil:
காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவினுக்கு
யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaadhalar thoodhodu vandha kanavinukku
yaadhusey vaenkol virundhu.
kurals.meaning: A dream came to me carrying a message from my absent beloved; what feast could I ever set before such a guest to thank it?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are missing a grandparent who lives far away, and one night you dream they send you a happy note saying they will visit soon. You wake up so glad that you want to thank the dream itself, as if it were a postman who knocked at your door with the best letter ever.
kurals.university: Chapter 122, kaṉavunilai uraittal (‘telling of the state of dreams’), continues the karpiyal sequence on separation: in the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the wife, long parted from her husband, tells her confidante (tōḻi) what she has seen in dreams, and the dreams become her way of enduring absence. The opening couplet personifies the dream as a guest who arrives with a tūtu (messenger, embassy), so that the hospitality word viruntu (feast offered to a guest, the virtue praised in Aṟam ch. 9) is turned on the dream itself; yātu ceyvēṉ-kol is a helpless rhetorical question, ‘what can I possibly do?’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss the line as asking what return (kaimmāṟu) she can make to the dream that came with her lover’s envoy. Pope renders: ‘It came and brought to me, that nightly vision rare, / A message from my love,- what feast shall I prepare?’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (which spells the chapter title as two words, kaṉavunilai uraittal).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the story of Nala and Damayanti, a golden swan that Nala has caught and released flies to Damayanti and praises Nala to her, carrying love between two people who have never met.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s tale makes a winged messenger the first bearer of love’s news between separated lovers.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s dream plays the same part as Nala’s swan: a go-between who brings the beloved’s message across distance, and earns the receiver’s gratitude.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the messenger motif fits, but the swan is a real bird, not a dream, and Damayanti does not ‘feast’ it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife.”
christianity.explanation: Matthew’s Gospel has a heavenly messenger arrive through a dream to settle Joseph’s anguish about the woman he is to marry.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a dream comes bearing a message about the beloved, and it changes the dreamer’s heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a real dream-messenger about a spouse, though the message comes from God rather than from the absent beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “If anyone of you sees a dream that he likes, then it is from Allah, and he should thank Allah for it and narrate it to others.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that a pleasing dream is a gift to be met with gratitude and shared.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise wants to repay a welcome dream; Islam directs that gratitude to God and asks the dreamer to tell it, much as she tells her confidante.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong fit on gratitude for a good dream, though the hadith is not about a lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A dream not interpreted is like a letter not read.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Hisda, quoted in the Talmud’s long discussion of dreams, treats a dream as a sealed message addressed to the dreamer.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s dream is exactly such a letter, arriving with the beloved’s envoy and waiting to be received with honour.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on the dream as a message, though the Talmud is concerned with interpretation, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Queen Maya dreams that a white elephant enters her side; on waking she tells King Suddhodana, who summons learned brahmins, feasts them generously and asks them to explain the dream, which they read as news of a great son to come.
buddhism.explanation: In the Buddhist birth narrative, a dream arrives as a herald of joyful tidings and is answered with lavish hospitality.
buddhism.tie_back: The royal feast given in thanks for Maya’s dream is the very kind of ‘viruntu’ the Kural’s heroine wishes she could offer her dream.
buddhism.source: Nidanakatha (Introduction to the Jataka), the conception of the Bodhisatta (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Birth Stories)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested narrative; the dream-as-herald and feast both match, though the tidings concern a birth, not a lover.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He accepted the true meaning of the dreams, and honoured the interpreters of dreams with praise and plenty of food, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.”
jainism.explanation: After Queen Trisala’s fourteen auspicious dreams foretell Mahavira’s birth, King Siddhartha thanks those who opened the dreams’ message with a lavish reception.
jainism.tie_back: Jain scripture shows the gratitude the Kural’s heroine longs to express: a dream bearing good news is answered with a feast.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §83 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong parallel of a feast in thanks for a dream’s message, though the honoured guests are interpreters, not the dream itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Penelope sleeps in grief, Athena sends a phantom in the likeness of her sister Iphthime, who stands over her head and comforts her with the message that her absent son Telemachus will return safely.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the anxious wife a dream-messenger sent from outside to carry word of an absent loved one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s dream-envoy is the Greek twin of the Kural’s dream ‘that came with my beloved’s messenger’.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 4.795-841 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; close match on a dream bringing news of an absent loved one, though it concerns a son rather than a husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In prison Socrates tells Crito he has dreamed of a fair woman in white who called him and spoke a line from Homer, telling him that on the third day he would come to fertile Phthia.
philosophy.explanation: Plato presents a dream as a gracious visitor delivering a message that Socrates trusts and acts upon.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates’ dream-woman, like the Kural’s dream, arrives as a courier from beyond and is welcomed rather than dismissed.
philosophy.source: Plato, Crito 44a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good fit on the dream as messenger, but its message concerns Socrates’ death, not love.

kurals.tamil:
கயலுண்கண் யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சிற் கலந்தார்க்கு
உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன் மன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kayalunkan yaanirappath thunjir kalandhaarkku
uyalunmai saatruvaen man.
kurals.meaning: If only my dark-lined, fish-shaped eyes would fall asleep when I beg them to, I could tell the one I love, when he comes in my dream, how I have barely managed to survive.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever had so much to tell someone that you lay awake and couldn’t sleep? This girl wants to fall asleep so she can meet her faraway husband in a dream and tell him how hard it has been, but the worry keeps her eyes wide open.
kurals.university: Kayal uṇ kaṇ, ‘carp-like eyes lined with collyrium’, is a stock Sangam image of feminine beauty, here made pathetic: the eyes that once drew the lover now refuse the sleep (tuñcil, ‘if they sleep’) that would let her meet him. Yāṉ irappa means ‘as I beg’, casting the heroine as a supplicant to her own eyes. Kalantārkku, ‘to him who united with me’, names the husband by their past union; uyal uṇmai is ‘the truth of my survival’, i.e. how she has scraped through the separation, and cāṟṟuvēṉ ‘I would declare’. The closing particle maṉ marks a wish that cannot be fulfilled, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan render as ‘I would tell him, if only’. Pope: ‘If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore, / The tale of my long-suffering life I’ll tell my loved one o’er.’ Both base sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Captive in Lanka, Sita entrusts Hanuman with a message for Rama telling him how she has endured, and warns that she can hold on to life only a little longer unless he comes.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda turns a separated wife’s account of her own survival into the message she most needs her husband to hear.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita’s message is what the Kural’s heroine longs to deliver, the ‘truth of how I have survived’, if only sleep would let her meet her husband.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Sita’s message to Rama through Hanuman (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good fit on telling the absent husband of one’s survival, though Sita speaks through a living messenger, not in a dream.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon lies awake at night seeking the beloved who is absent.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sleepless heroine, she spends the night on her bed searching for a meeting that will not come.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; close on night-time longing on one’s bed, though without the wish to sleep in order to speak.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, long separated from Joseph, will pour out his grief only before God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also has a tale of suffering she longs to pour out; she seeks a hearing from her beloved in sleep, where Jacob seeks it from God.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; shares the urge to voice the grief of separation, but the addressee is God, not the beloved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou holdest fast the lids of mine eyes; I am troubled, and cannot speak.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist lies awake in distress, his eyelids held open, unable to put his trouble into words.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s predicament exactly reversed into lament: sleeplessness that keeps one from speaking one’s sorrow.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on sleeplessness blocking speech, though the psalm’s grief is religious, not romantic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Asked whether he slept well on a cold night on leaves, the Buddha says he did, and explains that a householder in a fine bed may still lie awake, burned by fevers born of passion, while one who has let passion go sleeps at ease.
buddhism.explanation: The Hatthaka discourse ties sleeplessness directly to desire.
buddhism.tie_back: From a Buddhist angle, the Kural’s heroine cannot sleep for exactly this reason: her longing is the fever that keeps her eyes open.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.35, Hatthaka Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; explains her sleeplessness well, but Buddhism prescribes giving up the longing the Kural cherishes.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that one who becomes attached to beautiful forms through the eye brings misery on himself, never finding satisfaction and suffering when the object is absent.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces suffering to the senses’ attachment to what they love to see.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers precisely because her eyes are bound to a beloved they cannot see; Jainism would counsel loosening that attachment rather than seeking it in sleep.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 32 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard Jain teaching; only a next-best match, since Jainism diagnoses the longing as bondage rather than sharing it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A short lyric fragment traditionally attributed to Sappho says that the moon and the Pleiades have set, it is midnight, the hours pass, and the speaker lies alone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek lyric captures the lover lying awake through the hours of night without the beloved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shares that midnight vigil, with the added ache that sleep itself would bring her love to her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; authorship of the fragment is disputed and it does not mention dreams, so this is a next-best match on sleepless solitude.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle explains sleep as a natural seizing of the primary sense-faculty that renders it unable to function, arising from bodily processes rather than from choice.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, sleep is not something the will can summon; it comes by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine begs her eyes to sleep, and Aristotle explains why begging does not work: sleep is not under the will’s command.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Sleep and Waking (De Somno), Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; an analytic sidelight on the heroine’s plea rather than a parallel teaching about love.

kurals.tamil:
நனவினால் நல்கா தவரைக் கனவினால்
காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaa thavaraik kanavinaal
kaantalin unten uyir.
kurals.meaning: He shows me no kindness while I am awake, but because I see him in my dreams, my life still holds on.
kurals.elementary: Think of a plant on a windowsill that only gets a little sunlight each morning. It is just enough to keep it alive. For this woman, seeing her husband in dreams is that little bit of sunlight that keeps her going until he comes home.
kurals.university: The couplet sets up the chapter’s governing antithesis of naṉavu (waking) and kaṉavu (dream), each in the instrumental (naṉaviṉāl, kaṉaviṉāl, ‘by waking’, ‘by dream’). Nalkātavar, ‘he who does not grant grace’, from nalku (to show favour, bestow love), names the absent husband by his failure to come; the word recurs through the chapter (1214, 1217, 1219) and functions almost as an epithet. Kāṇṭaliṉ, ‘because of seeing’, gives the cause, and uṇṭu eṉ uyir, ‘my life exists’, makes the dream the slender thread on which her life hangs. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as ‘my life has not yet left me only because I see him in dreams’. Pope: ‘Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows, / In dreams I see; and so my lifetime goes!’ The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Bhasa’s play, King Udayana, believing his queen Vasavadatta dead, murmurs to her in his sleep; she, actually alive and in disguise nearby, gently touches him and slips away, and on waking he cannot tell whether he has dreamed her or truly seen her.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘Vision of Vasavadatta’ makes a dream the only place where a grieving husband can still meet his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Udayana, like the Kural’s heroine, is kept going by seeing in dreams the spouse whom waking life denies him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s famous dream scene; strong fit on the dream as the sustaining meeting-place of separated spouses, with the roles of the sexes reversed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
christianity.explanation: After a night of fruitless searching, the bride in the Song of Solomon at last finds her beloved and clings to him; many interpreters read the scene as a night-vision.
christianity.tie_back: Her finding the beloved after vain searching is the Kural’s dream-meeting, the encounter that keeps the seeker alive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; reading the scene as a dream is an interpretive tradition, not explicit in the text.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever sees me in a dream will see me in his wakefulness, and Satan cannot imitate me in shape.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet assures believers who long for him that seeing him in a dream is a true sight, a promise of meeting him in waking.
islam.tie_back: For the Kural’s heroine too, the dream-sight of the absent beloved is real enough to sustain her until waking union returns.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; parallel on dream-sight of a beloved figure as genuine, but the love is devotional, not marital.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh; Hark! my beloved knocketh: ‘Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled.’”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite, asleep, hears her beloved come to her door in what reads as a dream-visit.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the beloved comes to the sleeper when he cannot be had by day, and that visit keeps the heart awake and alive.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on the beloved’s visit in sleep, though the Song does not say the visit sustains her life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that from what is dear springs grief and from what is dear springs fear; for one wholly free from endearment there is no grief.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism sees the heart’s dependence on a loved one as the very source of sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine stakes her life on dream-glimpses of the beloved; the Buddhist verse explains why such dependence brings both her sustenance and her pain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a contrastive rather than parallel match, since Buddhism counsels release from the attachment the Kural celebrates.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Jain retellings of the Ramayana, Sita in Ravana’s captivity is sustained by unbroken fidelity to Rama and by the news of him that Hanuman brings.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative presents a separated wife whose constancy to an absent husband keeps her alive through captivity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise survives on the image of the husband who is not with her, though she finds it in dreams rather than in vows.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Jain Ramayana tradition, not verified line by line; only a next-best match, as no dream is involved.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Often you will gladden me, appearing in my dreams; for sweet it is to look on those we love in dreams, however brief the night.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Admetus, about to lose his wife Alcestis, consoles himself that she will still come to him in dreams.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comfort almost word for word: when waking life withholds the beloved, dream-sight keeps the lover going.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Alcestis 354-356 (tr. Richard Aldington, via the Internet Classics Archive)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; near one-to-one on the solace of seeing a lost spouse in dreams.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that dream-images are residual movements left in the sense-organs by earlier perceptions, which persist after the perceived object has gone and present themselves in sleep.
philosophy.explanation: On Aristotle’s account, the sight of an absent person survives within us after the person departs.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who no longer comes by day still reaches the Kural’s heroine at night because, as Aristotle explains, his image lingers in her.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Dreams (De Insomniis) 460b-461a, Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; an explanatory rather than emotional parallel to the Kural’s dream-sustained love.

kurals.tamil:
கனவினான் உண்டாகும் காமம் நனவினான்
நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kanavinaan undaakum kaamam nanavinaan
nalkaarai naatith thararku.
kurals.meaning: Love’s joy comes to me in dreams because the dream goes out, searches for the one who will not come to me in waking life, and brings him to me.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friendly dog that runs off every night and comes back pulling your best friend by the sleeve so you can play together. Here the dream is like that helpful dog: it goes and finds the husband who is far away and brings him home, just for the night.
kurals.university: Here the dream is not merely a place but an agent: nāṭi, ‘having searched out’, and taraṟku, ‘in order to give, bring’, make it a go-between who fetches the reluctant lover. The forms kaṉaviṉāṉ and naṉaviṉāṉ use the older instrumental ending -āṉ for -āl, a metrical variant noted in Tamil grammatical tradition. Kāmam here is the pleasure of love, not mere desire; nalkārai repeats the epithet ‘him who grants no grace’ from 1213. Varadarasanar reads the couplet as ‘love-incidents arise in dreams in order to seek out and bring the lover’, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar shift the stress to the joy the dream gives by bringing him. Pope: ‘Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not me / In waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Princess Usha sees in a dream a handsome youth she has never met and falls in love; her friend Chitralekha paints portraits until Usha recognises him as Aniruddha, Krishna’s grandson, and then by her yogic power fetches him from Dvaraka to Usha’s chamber.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana tells of a dream that first reveals the beloved and then leads to his being searched out and brought to the dreamer.
hinduism.tie_back: Usha’s dream, which ends with the beloved literally fetched to her side, is the Kural’s ‘dream that seeks him out and brings him’ made into narrative.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; near one-to-one on a dream that finds and brings the beloved, though a friend does the fetching.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: In the night-scene of the Song of Solomon, the bride rises from her bed to go searching the city for her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The night-search the bride undertakes is what the Kural’s dream does on the heroine’s behalf: it goes looking for the lover who does not come.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; strong match on the nocturnal search for the beloved, though here she searches herself and does not yet find him.

islam.quote_or_event: “O my father, this is the explanation of my vision of before. My Lord has made it reality.”
islam.explanation: Joseph, reunited at last with the father from whom he was torn, recognises in the reunion the fulfilment of his boyhood dream.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s dream finally brought the separated family together, as the Kural’s dream brings the absent husband to his wife.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; a dream that leads to reunion, but over years and in waking life, not nightly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person is shown in his dream only the thoughts of his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, teaches that dreams draw their images from the dreamer’s waking thoughts.
judaism.tie_back: This explains the Kural’s dream: the heart that dwells on the absent husband all day sends the dream to find him by night.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (bold text of the William Davidson rendering); strong explanatory fit, though the Talmud does not speak of love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nagasena tells King Milinda that dreams arise in six ways, among them from what the dreamer has been habitually occupied with, and from portents of what is to come.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist analysis recognises that the mind’s habitual preoccupations generate dream-images.
buddhism.tie_back: On Nagasena’s account, the Kural’s dream is fetched by the heroine’s own constant preoccupation with her husband.
buddhism.source: Milindapanha, the dilemma on dreams (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 36)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the standard translation, not verified line by line; explanatory rather than emotional parallel.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavati Sutra’s discussion of dreams distinguishes several kinds, including a dream that arises from what one has been thinking about while awake (cinta-svapna).
jainism.explanation: Jain canonical teaching recognises dreams produced by the waking mind’s preoccupations.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-dream that ‘seeks out’ the husband is, in Jain terms, a cinta-svapna born of her constant thought of him.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from secondary summaries of the Bhagavati’s dream typology, not verified against a live translation; explanatory only.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Juno sends Iris to the house of Sleep, who dispatches his son Morpheus to take the form of the drowned king Ceyx and stand by the bed of his longing wife Alcyone, so that she may see him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid has the god of dreams go out and fetch the absent husband’s likeness to his waiting wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Morpheus does exactly what the Kural’s dream does: he goes and brings the husband who cannot come in waking life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong fit on a dream sent to bring the husband, though Morpheus brings news of death, not love’s joy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Freud argues that, when the work of interpretation is completed, a dream proves to be the fulfilment of a wish.
philosophy.explanation: For Freud the dream stages the very satisfaction waking life withholds.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s dream, which supplies the love denied by day, is a textbook instance of Freud’s wish-fulfilling dream, stated two thousand years earlier.
philosophy.source: Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams, ch. 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.A. Brill)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Freud’s central thesis; strong conceptual fit, though Freud’s framework is clinical rather than poetic.

kurals.tamil:
நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ஆங்கே கனவுந்தான்
கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavinaal kandadhooum aange kanavundhaan
kanda pozhudhae inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Seeing him while awake was sweet only for as long as it lasted; seeing him in a dream is just as sweet, for the moment it is seen.
kurals.elementary: An ice-cream cone is lovely while you are eating it, and then it’s gone. A dream about someone you love is the same: it is just as lovely while it lasts. This woman says both kinds of seeing, awake and dreaming, are sweet, but only in the moment.
kurals.university: Kaṇṭatūum is kaṇṭatu, ‘what was seen’, with uyir-aḷapeṭai, the metrical prolongation of the vowel (-ūum) that Tamil prosody uses to fill out a foot. Āṅkē, ‘just then, at that time’, and kaṇṭa poḻutē, ‘at the very moment of seeing’, set the two experiences on a level: both sweetnesses are bounded by the moment. Varadarasanar stresses the limitation (‘only at that time… only at the time it is seen’), whereas Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress the equality (‘both were pleasures to me’); the couplet can carry both, a consolation tinged with the knowledge that waking joy too was fleeting. Pope: ‘As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet, / So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet.’ Both base sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mandukya Upanishad describes the dream state (taijasa) as a condition of consciousness turned inward that enjoys its own subtle objects, as the waking state enjoys gross ones.
hinduism.explanation: Vedantic analysis treats dreaming and waking as parallel states of experience, each with its own real enjoyment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same parity from the side of feeling: the dream-sight of her husband is enjoyed as fully as the waking one was.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a metaphysical parallel to the Kural’s emotional claim, not a teaching about love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon savours the sweetness of being near her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural measures dream-sight against exactly this remembered sweetness of being with the beloved, and finds it equal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the sweetness of presence but says nothing about dreams.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that nothing of prophethood remains after him except glad tidings, and explained these as good, true dreams.
islam.explanation: In the Sunni tradition, a good dream is a real portion of blessing granted to the believer.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise refuses to discount the dream: its sweetness is as real as waking joy.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Interpretation of Dreams, on al-mubashshirat (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; the hadith number was not verified this session, so none is given. Partial fit on dreams as genuine good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the LORD brought back those that returned to Zion, We were like unto them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist likens the joy of a longed-for homecoming to the joy of dreaming.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set dream-joy and real joy side by side as equally sweet, the psalm by simile, the Kural by experience.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; partial fit, since the psalm compares a real event to a dream rather than a dream to a real event.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The closing verse of the Diamond Sutra bids the disciple regard all conditioned things as a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, as dew or a flash of lightning.
buddhism.explanation: Mahayana teaching places waking experience and dreams on the same fleeting footing.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine arrives at the same parity, waking sweetness and dream sweetness both lasting only ‘while seen’, but she treasures what the sutra counsels letting go.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse; good conceptual fit on the equal transience of waking and dream, with opposite conclusions drawn.

jainism.quote_or_event: “These my excellent and pre-eminent dreams shall not be counteracted by other bad dreams.” Accordingly she remained awake to save her dreams by means of (hearing) good, auspicious, pious, agreeable stories about gods and religious men.
jainism.explanation: Queen Trisala treasures her auspicious dreams so much that she stays awake to keep their sweetness intact.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Trisala holds that a good dream is a real treasure whose sweetness belongs to the time it is seen and must be guarded.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §§54-55 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; parallel on cherishing a dream’s sweetness, though Trisala’s dreams are religious omens, not visions of a lover.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “This very night methought there was one lying by my side who was like Ulysses as he was when he went away with his host, and I rejoiced, for I believed that it was no dream, but the very truth itself.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope tells how, in a dream, her long-absent husband seemed beside her as he was when he left, and her joy was as full as if it were real.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim lived out: the dream-sight of the absent husband was, while it lasted, as sweet as waking union.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20 (tr. Samuel Butler, via the Internet Classics Archive)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; near one-to-one on dream-joy equal to waking joy, though Penelope also calls it a misery that haunts her.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Theaetetus how anyone could prove whether we are now asleep or awake, noting that in dreams we believe what we see just as firmly as in waking life.
philosophy.explanation: Plato observes that, at the time it is had, a dream experience carries the same conviction as waking experience.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the emotional version of Plato’s point: in the moment of seeing, dream and waking are equally sweet.
philosophy.source: Plato, Theaetetus 158b-d (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good conceptual fit on the parity of dream and waking ‘at the time’, framed epistemically rather than emotionally.

kurals.tamil:
நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின் கனவினால்
காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavena ondrillai aayin kanavinaal
kaadhalar neengalar man.
kurals.meaning: If there were no such thing as waking, my beloved, who comes to me in dreams, would never leave me.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever had a really happy dream and felt sad when the alarm clock rang? This woman wishes there were no alarm clock at all, no waking up, so that the husband she sees in her dreams could stay with her forever.
kurals.university: Naṉavu eṉa oṉṟu illai āyiṉ, ‘if there were no one thing called waking’, is a bold counterfactual that makes waking itself the villain; Pappaiah even calls it ‘a cruel sinner’ (koṭiya pāvi), and Kalaignar has it ‘suddenly coming to spoil’ the meeting. Nīṅkalar, ‘he would not depart’, describes the lover in the dream, and the final particle maṉ again marks an impossible wish, as in 1212. The couplet inverts the common wisdom that dreams are unreal and waking true: for the heroine, waking is what takes the beloved away. Pope: ‘And if there were no waking hour, my love / In dreams would never from my side remove.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that in dreams there are no chariots, horses or roads, yet the self creates chariots, horses and roads, joys and delights, for itself, being their maker.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad describes the dream-world as one the self fashions and fully inhabits while it lasts.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes she could live wholly in that self-made world where her beloved never departs.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; good fit on the dream as a complete world, though the Upanishad’s aim is metaphysical, not romantic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Solomon repeatedly asks that love not be roused before its time, guarding a blissful repose.
christianity.tie_back: Her plea not to wake echoes the Kural’s wish that waking would never come to break the lovers’ union.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the ‘do not awaken’ refrain is commonly read as about love’s timing, so the match on waking is partly verbal.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die [He takes] during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes sleep as a temporary taking of the soul, released again at waking.
islam.tie_back: For the Kural’s heroine the soul’s nightly absence is where she meets her beloved; its release into waking is the parting she laments.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; a theological frame for sleep and waking rather than a parallel teaching on love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be as when a hungry man dreameth, and, behold, he eateth, But he awaketh, and his soul is empty.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah’s image captures the dreamer who is satisfied in sleep and left empty on waking.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: in the dream the beloved is present, and waking leaves her empty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on waking as the loss of dream-fulfilment, though Isaiah’s image serves a prophecy about nations.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a man doesn’t see, on awakening, what he met in a dream, even so he doesn’t see, when they are dead, their time done, those he held dear.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the vanishing of dream-companions at waking as the image of how loved ones are lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the same experience from inside: waking is what makes the beloved met in the dream disappear.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 4.6, Jara Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong match on waking erasing the dream-beloved, though the Buddha draws a lesson of non-attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra contrasts the unwise, who sleep, with the sages, who are always awake, making wakefulness the mark of spiritual life.
jainism.explanation: Jain scripture prizes vigilance and treats ‘sleep’ as delusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes waking away; Jainism, by contrast, would call her dream-bound love the true sleep from which one must awake.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a contrastive match only, since Jainism values the waking the Kural laments.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The ghost of Patroclus comes to Achilles in his sleep and asks for burial; Achilles stretches out his arms to embrace his friend, but the spirit vanishes like smoke beneath the earth, and Achilles springs up awake in amazement.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows the beloved met in sleep slipping away at the very moment the dreamer reaches for him and wakes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ lost embrace is what the Kural’s heroine fears every dawn: waking is what makes the beloved leave.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 23.65-107 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; strong fit on waking as the loss of the dream-beloved, though the bond is comradeship and the friend is dead.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal remarks that if we dreamed the same thing every night, it would affect us as much as the objects we see every day; it is chiefly the continuity of waking life that makes us call it real.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal suggests that what separates dream from waking is only waking’s steady continuity.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural imagines removing that very continuity, abolishing waking, so that the dream-beloved would become her whole reality.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; fragment numbering differs between editions; good conceptual fit on dreams that would rival waking reality.

kurals.tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார் கனவனால்
என்எம்மைப் பீழிப் பது.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaak kotiyaar kanavanaal
en-emmaip peezhip padhu.
kurals.meaning: The hard-hearted one who will not show me grace while I am awake: why does he come in my dreams only to torment me?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who never answers your calls in the daytime but keeps popping up in your dreams. You might grumble, ‘If you won’t come and play when I’m awake, why do you keep visiting me at night and making me miss you even more?’
kurals.university: The mood turns from gratitude to reproach. Koṭiyār, ‘the cruel one’ (honorific plural), is a lover’s accusation, and pīḻippatu, ‘tormenting’, from pīḻ (to afflict, squeeze), names the pain of a dream that teases without fulfilling. Eṉ is the interrogative ‘why’, and emmai the plural ‘us’, the heroine speaking of herself with the inclusive dignity common in akam speech. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print kaṉavaṉāl in the first line, where many editions have the regular instrumental kaṉaviṉāl; the sense is unaffected. Kalaignar glosses the torment as the dream ‘enlarging the grief of separation’. Pope: ‘The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems, / Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams?’

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa’s exiled yaksha tells his wife, through the cloud, that when at last he finds her in a dream and stretches his arms into empty air to embrace her, even the forest deities shed tears like pearls at his plight.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘Cloud Messenger’ dwells on the cruelty of a dream-meeting that ends in arms closing on nothing.
hinduism.tie_back: The yaksha’s empty embrace is the torment the Kural’s heroine complains of: a lover who comes in dreams only to leave her more bereft.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta, Uttaramegha (paraphrase; verse number varies by recension)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous stanza; strong fit on the pain of a dream-embrace, though here it is the husband who suffers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions.”
christianity.explanation: Job finds that even the refuge of sleep becomes a place of torment through dreams.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same complaint: the night that should console her brings dreams that afflict.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; strong match on tormenting dreams, though Job’s affliction comes from God and not from a lover.

islam.quote_or_event: “[It is but] a mixture of false dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams.”
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s courtiers dismiss his troubling dream as a jumble of confused visions.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine might wish to dismiss her teasing dreams the same way, but they torment her precisely because they feel real.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; only a partial fit on troubling dreams, and the courtiers turn out to be wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: Shmuel, when he saw a bad dream, would say “And the dreams speak falsely” (Zechariah 10:2); when he saw a good dream, he would ask whether dreams speak falsely, citing “I speak with him in a dream” (Numbers 12:6).
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a sage who answered distressing dreams by declaring them empty and welcomed good ones as true.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is caught between those two attitudes: the dream-lover delights her, yet torments her because he will not come in truth.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a passage read on Sefaria (the scripture citations are verbatim); a partial fit on ambivalence toward dreams.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Potaliya discourse the Buddha compares sensual pleasures to a dream: a man dreams of delightful parks, groves and lakes, but on waking sees none of them.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism uses the dream to show how pleasures promise satisfaction and leave nothing behind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels exactly this cheat: the dream gives her the beloved and then leaves her with nothing, which is why she calls it torment.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 54, Potaliya Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nanamoli and Bodhi)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile; good fit on dream-pleasure that does not last, though Buddhism concludes one should renounce such pleasures.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Citta and Sambhuta, the monk Citta warns his brother, now a pleasure-loving king, that all pleasures in the end bring pain and that delight in them is empty.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that pleasures, however sweet, carry their own suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers this at night: the pleasure of the dream-lover is itself what pains her.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 13, Citta and Sambhuta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a next-best match, since Jainism’s answer is renunciation rather than complaint.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that dreams pass through two gates: those that come through the gate of ivory deceive and bring words that are never fulfilled, while those through the gate of horn come true.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the separated wife a theory of deceiving dreams that promise what waking does not deliver.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘cruel one’ who comes only in dreams is just such an ivory-gate dream, sweet in sleep and false by day.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.560-567 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; good fit on dreams that tease with unfulfilled promise, told by a wife longing for her husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius compares lovers to a thirsty man who in sleep seeks to drink and is given only images of water, so that he thirsts still while drinking; so Venus mocks lovers with images that never satisfy.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, love fed on images, above all in dreams, inflames longing instead of quenching it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine suffers exactly this: the dream-image of her husband torments because it cannot satisfy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong fit on dream-images that torment the lover, though Lucretius advises escaping love altogether.

kurals.tamil:
துஞ்சுங்கால் தோள்மேலர் ஆகி விழிக்குங்கால்
நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunjungaal thoalmelar aaki vizhikkungaal
nenjaththar aavar viraindhu.
kurals.meaning: When I sleep, he rests upon my shoulders; the moment I wake, he quickly slips into my heart.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kitten that naps on your shoulder, and when you sit up it darts inside your jacket to stay warm. The husband in this poem is like that: in sleep he is right beside her, and when she wakes up he hurries to hide in her heart, so he is never really gone.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most celebrated couplet for its grace. Tuñcuṅkāl / viḻikkuṅkāl (‘when I sleep’ / ‘when I wake’) frame a perfect parallel, and tōḷmēlar (‘he who is on my shoulders’) answers neñcattar (‘he who is in my heart’), so that the beloved merely changes residence and is never absent. Viraintu, ‘swiftly’, gives the image a playful quickness, as if he darts inward at the first stir of waking. Pappaiah reads it as ‘my lord, who always lives in my heart, lies on my shoulder when I sleep’, while Kalaignar stresses that on waking ‘he went nowhere, but leapt into my heart and settled there’. The couplet softens the reproach of 1217 into consolation. Pope: ‘And when I sleep he holds my form embraced; / And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste!’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna sends word to the gopis of Vraja through Uddhava that he is never really separated from them, and that he stays far away so that their minds may dwell on him all the more constantly.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana teaches that the absent beloved is held all the closer within the heart of the one who longs.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband who ‘hastens into the heart’ on waking is Krishna’s message in miniature: absence becomes indwelling.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; strong fit on the absent beloved dwelling in the heart, within a devotional rather than marital frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song of Solomon pictures her beloved holding her as she rests.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural’s picture, the beloved resting close as she sleeps; the Kural adds that on waking he moves into her heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the restful embrace but lacks the Kural’s turn to the heart on waking.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that God, though unseen, is nearer to a person than his own life-vein.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved, unseen by day yet lodged within the heart, is near in this same intimate, invisible way.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; parallel on unseen inner nearness, applied to God rather than a spouse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death.”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite asks to be impressed on her beloved’s heart and arm, so that she is never separate from him.
judaism.tie_back: Heart and arm in the Song match heart and shoulder in the Kural: the beloved is borne on the body and sealed within.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on the beloved held on the body and in the heart, without the sleep/waking contrast.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dvedhavitakka discourse the Buddha teaches that whatever one frequently thinks and ponders becomes the inclination of one’s mind.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism observes that sustained attention shapes what the mind turns to of its own accord.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved leaps into the heart the moment she wakes because, as the Buddha notes, the mind turns by habit to what it dwells on.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 19, Dvedhavitakka Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known teaching; an explanatory parallel, since the sutta aims to redirect such habits toward renunciation.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Neminatha abandons his wedding procession to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati, keeping him in her heart, refuses another match and herself takes vows, following him on the path.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative tells of a bride whose devotion to an absent bridegroom becomes the guiding presence of her life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati, like the Kural’s heroine, carries the departed beloved within; Jainism turns that inner presence toward renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22, Rathanemi (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative; partial fit on the absent beloved held in the heart, redirected to ascetic ends.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s myth of the winged soul, the lover parted from the beloved is in anguish, but the memory of the beloved’s beauty, held within, gives him joy, and he longs to return to his side.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Phaedrus makes the beloved’s image, kept in the soul, the lover’s consolation in absence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved who moves from shoulder to heart is the same inward image that sustains Plato’s lover between meetings.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251d-252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a mythic passage; good fit on the beloved held within during absence, set in a philosophical allegory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle compares memory to the impression a signet-ring leaves in wax, a lasting imprint of what was once perceived.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, those we have known leave a stamp in the soul that remains after they are gone.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who ‘hastens into the heart’ the moment she wakes is such an imprint, always present to recall.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, On Memory (De Memoria) 450a, Parva Naturalia (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; an analytic parallel to the Kural’s image, without its tenderness.

kurals.tamil:
நனவினால் நல்காரை நோவர் கனவினால்
காதலர்க் காணா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavinaal nalkaarai noavar kanavinaal
kaadhalark kaanaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Only women who never see their lovers in dreams grieve over, and blame, the men who do not come to them in waking life.
kurals.elementary: Suppose your friend moved away, but you write letters every week. Someone who has never had a pen pal might say, ‘Your friend forgot you!’ But you know better, because you hear from them all the time. This woman says the same about her dreams: people who don’t have such dreams just don’t understand.
kurals.university: The heroine turns outward to defend her husband against criticism. Nōvar, ‘they grieve over / reproach’, has as subject kaṉaviṉāl kātalark kāṇātavar, ‘those who do not see their lovers through dreams’; nalkārai repeats the chapter’s epithet for the man who ‘shows no grace’. The implication is that her own dreams vindicate him, since he visits her every night. Commentators differ on whom she means: Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it general (‘women who do not see their lovers in dreams’), while Pappaiah specifies the young women of the town who are unmarried or have never known separation and so blame her husband as loveless. Pope: ‘In dreams who ne’er their lover’s form perceive, / For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Uddhava, sent by Krishna to console the gopis with philosophy, is humbled by the depth of their love for the absent Krishna and comes to wish he could be even a creeper in Vrindavan touched by the dust of their feet.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana shows an outsider, learned but untouched by such love, misjudging the gopis until he sees their devotion from within.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the critics in the Kural, Uddhava first speaks without knowing the inner experience of the lovers; once he sees it, his view reverses.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good fit on outsiders who cannot understand a love they have not experienced, though Uddhava does not blame Krishna.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm describes sleep itself as a gift given to those who are beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees her dream-visits as such a gift; those who lack it are left with ‘the bread of sorrows’ and complaint.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a loose next-best match on sleep as a gift to the beloved, without the theme of blame.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons, who do not share his bond with Joseph, chide him for his unceasing longing.
islam.tie_back: Like the critics in the Kural, Jacob’s sons judge a love they do not share and cannot see from inside.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; good fit on outsiders reproaching a lover’s longing, though they blame the one who longs, not the absent one.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Zeira says that anyone who sleeps seven days without a dream is called evil, since it suggests that God does not wish to appear to him even in that indirect way.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud treats an absence of dreams as a sign of estrangement from the divine.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly marks those who do not dream of their beloved as the ones who lack the bond, and who therefore misjudge.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a passage read on Sefaria; a partial match on dreamlessness as a sign of distance, with a religious rather than romantic sense.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, mad with grief, carries her dead child from house to house seeking medicine; told to fetch mustard seed from a house where no one has died, she finds none and comes to understand loss from within.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist story shows that understanding of another’s sorrow comes only from shared experience.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s critics blame her husband because they have no share in her dream-experience; Kisa Gotami learns compassion only when she sees her grief is common to all.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 114 / Therigatha commentary, Kisa Gotami (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.W. Burlingame)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous story; only a next-best match on understanding through shared experience, with no lover involved.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Seeing that these fourteen illustrious, beautiful, lucky, blest, auspicious, fortunate, great dreams were taken from her by the Kshatriyani Trisala, she awoke.”
jainism.explanation: The Brahmani Devananda, from whose womb the embryo of Mahavira is transferred, wakes to find her auspicious dreams have passed to another woman.
jainism.tie_back: Devananda is the Jain picture of one who has lost her blessed dreams; the Kural notes that it is those without such dreams who grieve and complain.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); only a next-best match on loss of blessed dreams, with no lover involved.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The suitor Agelaus tells Telemachus that while there was hope of Odysseus returning, Penelope’s waiting was understandable, but that it is now clear he will never come home, and she should marry the best of the suitors.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives voice to outsiders who, not sharing Penelope’s hope, declare the absent husband gone for good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agelaus is the Kural’s critic in action, judging the absent husband lost because he cannot see what keeps the wife’s faith alive.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 20 (paraphrase of the Samuel Butler translation)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a passage read on classics.mit.edu; good fit on outsiders pronouncing the absent husband lost.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we have no immediate experience of what others feel and can form an idea of it only by imagining ourselves in their situation.
philosophy.explanation: For Smith, sympathy depends on imaginatively entering another’s circumstances.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s critics, never having been visited by a lover in dreams, cannot enter the heroine’s situation, and so they misjudge her husband.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Smith’s opening argument; an explanatory parallel on the limits of judging an experience one has not had.

kurals.tamil:
நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர் கனவினால்
காணார்கொல் இவ்வூ ரவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanavinaal namneeththaar enpar kanavinaal
kaanaarkol ivvoo ravar.
kurals.meaning: The people of this town say he has abandoned me in waking life; do they not see him coming to me in my dreams?
kurals.elementary: Imagine the neighbours saying, ‘Poor girl, her friend never visits.’ But every night her friend calls her on a secret walkie-talkie. She thinks, ‘They just can’t hear what I hear!’ That is how this woman feels about the town’s gossip.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by setting the heroine’s private knowledge against public opinion (alar, the town’s gossip that runs through the Kāmattuppāl). Nam nīttār eṉpar, ‘they say he has forsaken us’, reports the townsfolk’s verdict; ivvūravar, ‘the people of this town’, are the critics already glimpsed in 1219. The particle kol makes kāṇārkol a wondering question, ‘do they not see?’, which can be read two ways: Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it as ‘do they not know that he visits me in dreams?’, whereas Kalaignar turns it back on the townsfolk, ‘do they never see their own departed lovers in dreams?’ Either way the dream, invisible to others, is her proof of his faithfulness. Pope: ‘They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone; / In dreams they surely see him not,- these people of the town.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Sita’s return to Ayodhya, the townspeople whisper doubts about her, unaware of the fidelity she kept through captivity, and Rama, hearing of the talk, bows to public opinion.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana’s final book dramatises the cruelty of town gossip that cannot see a wife’s inner truth.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk likewise pronounce judgement on a marriage whose real life, here the nightly dream-visits, they cannot see.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, the townspeople’s gossip about Sita (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; partial fit on gossip misjudging a couple, though the gossip targets the wife, not the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?”
christianity.explanation: The daughters of Jerusalem, not sharing the bride’s love, question why she prizes an absent beloved so highly.
christianity.tie_back: They are the Kural’s ‘people of this town’: outsiders puzzled by a devotion whose grounds they cannot see.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; good fit on onlookers questioning a lover’s faith in the absent beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind.” They said, “By Allah, indeed you are in your [same] old error.”
islam.explanation: Jacob senses his long-lost son is near, and those around him dismiss his inner certainty as an old delusion.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same scepticism: she knows her beloved has not truly left her, while the town sees only his absence.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via quran.com API; strong fit on private certainty against public dismissal, with a father and son rather than spouses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they said one to another: ‘Behold, this dreamer cometh.’”
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s brothers mock him as ‘the master of dreams’, scorning visions they do not share.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk, likewise dismissing what is seen only in dreams, are blind to the truth the dreamer holds.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; partial match on outsiders scorning a dreamer, without the theme of an absent lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells of blind men who each touch one part of an elephant and then quarrel, each sure the whole elephant is like the part he felt.
buddhism.explanation: The parable warns against confident judgements formed from a partial view.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk see only the waking half of the marriage and confidently declare the husband gone, missing the nightly half.
buddhism.source: Udana 6.4, Tittha Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous parable; an analogical fit on partial knowledge, not a teaching about love.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain epistemology teaches that reality is known through valid knowledge and partial standpoints (nayas), and that any single standpoint, taken as the whole truth, misleads.
jainism.explanation: Anekantavada warns that judgements formed from one angle grasp only part of a many-sided reality.
jainism.tie_back: The townsfolk judge the marriage from the single standpoint of waking life; the Kural’s heroine knows a second standpoint that changes the verdict.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6 and 1.33 on pramana and naya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a central Jain doctrine; an analogical match on partial viewpoints, not about love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, whose husband Protesilaus fell at Troy, keeps a likeness of him in her chamber and embraces it; a servant who glimpses this reports that she has a lover, and her father, misunderstanding, has the image burned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows outsiders misreading a wife’s private communion with her absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Laodamia’s household, the Kural’s townsfolk see only the outside and misjudge a love whose real life is hidden from them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a mythographic summary; good fit on onlookers misreading a wife’s private bond with an absent husband.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus is reported as saying that the waking share one common world, whereas each sleeper turns aside into a private world of his own.
philosophy.explanation: The fragment marks the dream as a world others cannot enter or verify.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s townsfolk live only in the common waking world; the heroine’s husband visits her in the private world Heraclitus describes, which they cannot see.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragment B89 Diels-Kranz, reported by Plutarch (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong conceptual fit on the dream as a private world closed to onlookers.
